cover.title:
Reverse
**Pairs**

blocks.label: HOW MANY PAIRS WITH LEFT > 2 × RIGHT?

cover.promise: You'll solve **LeetCode 493** in O(n log n).

slides.teaser: The problem, as a line of kids
slides.title: Giants in the line
slides.scene: This is Reverse Pairs, told as kids in a line. A kid is a giant to anyone behind them who is less than half their height.

blocks.text: 6 is a giant to the 1 and to the 2 behind it. How many giant pairs are there in the whole line?

slides.title: LeetCode 493
slides.lead: Count the pairs i < j with nums[i] > 2 × nums[j].

blocks.text: Up to 50,000 values, each anywhere in the 32-bit range.

slides.try_first: Find the {{TOTAL}} pairs of [6, 4, 1, 5, 2] by hand, then ask how to skip checking all {{ALL_PAIRS}}.

slides.title: Check every pair
slides.lead: For each value, compare it with every value after it.

blocks.label: THE SLOW WAY, FOR 6
blocks.note: Compare 6 with 4, 1, 5 and 2. Then do the same for 4, for 1, and so on.

blocks.text: n(n − 1)/2 checks: over a billion at 50,000 values.

slides.title: Sorted halves help
slides.lead: Split the line in two. If both halves were sorted, the pairs across them line up neatly.

blocks.text: 6 > 2 × 2, and any bigger left value pairs with 2 too.

quickcheck.question: Left half 3 7 9, right half 1 4, both sorted. How many pairs across?

slides.title: Use merge sort
slides.lead: Merge sort from post 25 already splits the line and hands you sorted halves before every merge.

blocks.text: Pairs inside each half: the same problem, smaller. Pairs across: count them, then merge.

slides.title: One walk across
slides.lead: For each right value r, skip left values ≤ 2 × r. Every left value after that pairs with r.

blocks.label: r = 2, SO SKIP LEFT VALUES ≤ 4
blocks.note: 6 is left, so 2 adds 1 pair. For r = 5, 6 ≤ 10: nothing.

blocks.text: r only grows, so i never walks back. Keep 2 × r in 64 bits.

final.caption: {{TOTAL}} pairs, and the line is sorted as a bonus.

slides.title: Split and recurse
slides.lead: Count inside each half with the same function. A single value has no pairs.

after.text: After the two calls, both halves come back sorted.

lines: for j from mid + 1 to high:
while i <= mid and nums[i] <= twice:
merge the two sorted halves   // post 25

items.label: Time
items.note: log n levels, one O(n) walk and merge each.

slides.pattern: Merge sort that counts pairs across the halves before each merge.

problems.title: Count of Smaller Numbers After Self
problems.note: Count-then-merge again, carrying each value's index.

blog.summary: To count pairs where an earlier value breaks a size rule against a later one, count across merge sort's sorted halves before each merge.
blog.tested_inputs: hand-picked cases (one value, two values, the LeetCode examples, sorted, reversed, all equal, negatives, zeros, and values at both 32-bit limits where 2 × value overflows 32 bits), one array of 2,000 random 32-bit values, random arrays of up to 14 small values and random arrays of up to 30 values from the whole 32-bit range
blog.tested_against: a brute force that checks every pair
blog.tested_extra: The pair counts at each merge and the quick-check answer come from running the code.

caption.first: LeetCode 493 Reverse Pairs solved with merge sort: count pairs across the sorted halves, then merge, in O(n log n).
lines: Checking every pair is O(n²). Once both halves are sorted, one walk counts every pair across them.
Keep 2 × nums[j] in 64 bits: values go up to 2³¹ − 1.
Practice next: LeetCode 315, the same idea with indexes.
